source.title: A Mechanistic Interpretability Analysis of Grokking

record.tranche_reason: The author trains small models on algorithmic tasks with restricted data and weight decay, and reports delayed generalization, similar in kind to the original grokking intervention. The post also measures circuit development during training.
record.gate_note: The post reports results on modular addition, 5-digit addition, and repeated-subsequence prediction. It also describes phase changes on other toy tasks, but does not give a distinct numerical or explicit outcome for each task in the text. Results cited from other work, including induction-head results, are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: This is Nanda's 2022 Alignment Forum post, the earlier version of original source arXiv:2301.05217. It trains small transformers on modular addition and other algorithmic tasks, reports delayed generalization, and tracks Fourier-circuit progress measures. It also reports a weight-decay comparison, a float64 log_softmax control, and replications across seeds and architectures. Because it is an early version of an original source, it gets no verdicts on V1 or V2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The author also claims the modular-addition model is fully reverse-engineered as a Fourier/trig-identity algorithm. He says circuit progress well before grokking disproves the random-walk hypothesis. He reduces grokking to phase change plus regularization plus limited data, and calls the phase-change explanations speculative.
record.recipe_differences: The post trains small algorithmic models with restricted data and weight decay, but focuses on mechanistic analysis of circuits and progress measures. Its modular-addition model is a 1L Transformer with no LayerNorm, width 128, AdamW, and full-batch training.
record.method_sensitivity: Weight decay changes the time to grok: 0.01 takes 60x as long as 1 in the reported modular-addition setting. The post also reports that float32 precision affects slingshot loss spikes, while casting logits to float64 fixes that issue without making slingshots necessary for grokking.

fits_no_version.finding: Given enough or infinite data, toy tasks show phase changes in both train and test loss. The tasks are modular addition at 95% data, 5-digit addition with per-digit phase changes, skip trigrams and repeated subsequences.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking arises when a task that shows phase changes is trained with regularization and limited data.

record.problems: Evidence is from tiny toy models. The author gives no systematic training-set-size sweep for grokking delay, says the crossover point was found by hand, and notes that only modular addition was fully interpreted. Several broader explanations are speculative.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for phase-change results on 5-digit addition with infinite data, skip trigrams, or maximum-element finding: the post describes these as phase changes but does not provide a distinct numerical or explicit outcome for each in the text. Cited induction-head and other external results are not rows.

untested.parts: No systematic sweep showing the delay grows as the training set shrinks. Only qualitative endpoints are given: 95% data gives a phase change without grokking, and a hand-found crossover.
Ungrokking below the critical dataset size is not tested. The crossover dataset size was found by hand and is not predicted from circuit efficiency.
Whether adaptive-optimizer (Adam) instability produces the delay is listed only as a future direction. SGD is not tested.
Seed consistency is checked informally ('several models, but not exhaustively'). No systematic comparison across hyperparameters.
Not tested; the author argues grokking is probably not relevant to large-model pretraining.

missing.what: Modular addition trained on 95% of the data shows a simultaneous phase change in train and test loss, with no grokking delay. This is a qualitative endpoint of how delay depends on data size.
Crossover dataset size between memorizing and generalizing (700 examples for 5-digit addition), found by binary search. Grokking appears just above this point.
missing.locator: Grokking = Phase Changes + Regularisation + Limited Data

missing.what: A 2L MLP replication groks modular addition and learns the same Fourier algorithm. Frequencies vary between seeds, and 5-digit addition preliminarily uses a variant of the trig algorithm.
missing.locator: Meta > 2L MLPs can grok modular addition; footnote 20; Future Directions

missing.what: With minibatch training in float64, loss spikes still occur, though rarer and less severe.

record.verdict_notes: This post is the precursor of original source arXiv:2301.05217, as the post itself states. No verdicts are given for V1 or V2, which that source defines; rows r1–r7 are kept for traceability only. The reader's V1/V2 'supports' labels are dropped. The V6 verdicts rest on text without rows and are anecdotal. Results come from tiny toy models with no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: The post does not report a systematic comparison showing that delay grows as the training set shrinks.
The detailed gradual-progress measurements are for modular addition; the post does not establish that this mechanism applies generally to other tasks.

The post speculates about phase changes in larger models and mentions cited work, but does not test grokking on non-algorithmic data or vary initialization scale or weight norm to switch it on or off.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning experiment on realistic data is reported.
The post argues that weight decay favors the generalizing solution and reports a weight-decay comparison, but does not establish a critical dataset size or systematically test ungrokking below it.
The post does not systematically compare identifiable algorithms across runs, architectures, or hyperparameters.
The post tests a float32 log_softmax precision issue and whether slingshots are necessary; it does not establish whether adaptive-optimizer instability produces the grokking delay.

rows.subject: 1L Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Trained on modular addition mod 113 with AdamW and weight decay 1.
rows.value: Training loss drops dramatically and then plateaus; test loss rises, remains high through the interpolation period, and falls during the later generalization phase (epochs 9K–13K).
rows.locator: Modular Addition; Evolution of Circuits During Training
rows.note: The account describes delayed test-loss improvement after the model has memorized the training data; it does not give a chance-accuracy number.
rows.check: Training-set size is garbled: '1132 pairs' is 113^2. The model is trained on 30% of 113^2 (about 3,830 pairs), not 1,132 pairs.

rows.subject: 1L Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Trained on 5-digit addition with weight decay and restricted data.
rows.value: Training loss plateaus at 3×10−8; test loss plateaus at 0.2; the post identifies the curve as grokking.
rows.locator: Grokking = Phase Changes + Regularisation + Limited Data
rows.note: The post does not state an accuracy or chance-level test value for this run.

rows.subject: 2L attention-only transformer

conditions.value: predicting repeated subsequences in random-token sequences

rows.value: The loss curve is described as showing clear grokking.
rows.note: The text does not give numerical loss or accuracy values for this curve.

rows.subject: 1L Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Tracked excluded loss by removing selected Fourier terms from the logits and measuring training loss.
rows.measure: Excluded loss relative to training loss
rows.value: Excluded loss smoothly diverges from training loss, indicating that the generalizing algorithm contributes increasingly to training performance before the test-loss change.
rows.note: The author describes excluded loss as a progress measure for the generalizing circuit.

rows.subject: 1L Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Restricted output logits to the directions for the five relevant frequencies and measured trig loss.
rows.measure: Trig loss on training and test data
rows.value: Trig loss shows a phase change; training and test trig-loss lines are described as almost equal and visually identical.
rows.note: The post interprets this metric as performance with the memorizing circuit removed and the generalizing circuit preserved.
rows.check: Trig loss isolates the generalizing circuit; it is not test accuracy. It bears on V2, not on V1's accuracy jump, so V1 is removed.

rows.subject: 1L Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Tracked test loss during the transition from memorization to generalization.
rows.value: A phase change in test loss follows the phase change in trig loss by a slight delay.
rows.note: The post attributes the delay to needing both a strong generalizing circuit and removal of the memorizing circuit.

rows.subject: 1L Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Tracked embedding norms for Fourier waves during training.
rows.value: The embedding norms have begun to become sparse.
rows.note: This is reported as progress toward the Fourier-based generalizing circuit before the test-performance transition.

rows.subject: 1L Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Compared grokking under two weight-decay settings.
rows.value: It groks, but takes 60x as long as weight decay 1.
rows.note: The author says lower weight decay delays grokking rather than stopping it.
rows.check: Varying weight decay does not test V1's dependence on training-set size, so V1 is removed. The row bears on V5's regularization account only.

rows.subject: 1L Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Repeated the training setup while casting logits to float64 before log_softmax.
rows.baseline: Training without this casting has slingshots attributed to a float32 precision error.
rows.value: Slingshots are not necessary to achieve grokking; the post says float64 casting fixes the precision issue.
rows.note: This argues against the claim that the numerical slingshot artifact is necessary for grokking. It does not test whether adaptive-optimizer instability causes the delay.
rows.check: Measure label: the slingshot spikes are removed by the float64 cast, but grokking still occurs. The V7 effect (delay vanishing under numerical control) is therefore absent. The text gives no numbers for this run.

relationships.condition: Modular addition mod 113, 30% data, weight decay 0.01 vs 1
relationships.reason: Lower weight decay still yields grokking but takes 60x as long (r8), consistent with weight decay driving the switch to the generalizing circuit. A data crossover point was also found (text, no row).
relationships.display_finding: Weight decay of 0.01 still yielded grokking but took 60 times as long as weight decay of 1; the study also identified a data crossover point.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Modular addition mod 113, 30% data, weight decay 0.01 vs 1
source_check.reason: Meta / Weight Decay explicitly reports grokking taking 60 times as long with weight decay 0.01 versus 1 and interprets this through the lower-weight generalizing solution.

relationships.condition: Full-batch AdamW, logits cast to float64 before log_softmax
relationships.reason: Removing the float32 softmax precision error removes the slingshot spikes, yet grokking still occurs (r9). The numerical artifact is not what produces the delay.
relationships.display_finding: Removing float32 softmax precision errors eliminated Slingshot spikes while preserving grokking, showing that this artifact did not produce the delay.

source_check.condition: Full-batch AdamW, logits cast to float64 before log_softmax
source_check.reason: The reported numerical correction fixes slingshots while grokking persists, contradicting disappearance of the delay under this control. It does not control all adaptive-optimizer effects.

relationships.reason: Based on text, no row: a replicated 2L MLP 'learned the same algorithm', the same Fourier multiplication method as the transformer.
relationships.display_finding: The replicated two-layer MLP learned the same Fourier multiplication method as the one-layer transformer.
